cards.explanation: The answer is that the gold has become dull. The poet says, "How the gold has become tarnished, the pure gold has become dull!" (Lamentations 4:1). Gold is supposed to shine, and this gold has lost it. I think that's why the poem opens with "How," like he can hardly believe what he's looking at. The gold is still there, but its shine is gone.

The answer is jars of clay. The poet says Zion's precious sons, "…once worth their weight in pure gold, are now esteemed as jars of clay, the work of a potter’s hands!" (Lamentations 4:2). That's a long drop from gold to clay, friends. It's a hard picture of how low they've fallen.

The answer is cruel. The poet says, "Even jackals offer their breasts to nurse their young, but the daughter of my people has become cruel, like an ostrich in the wilderness." (Lamentations 4:3). A jackal is a wild animal, and even it feeds its young. He's saying his own people have fallen below that. It's a hard thing to say about your own.

The answer is False. Nobody gives them any. The poet says, "Little children beg for bread, but no one gives them any." (Lamentations 4:4). They ask, and nobody hands them a thing. It's a heavy one, friends. He doesn't say why, and I won't guess.

The answer is in ash heaps. The poet says, "those brought up in crimson huddle in ash heaps." (Lamentations 4:5). Crimson was the color of how they were raised, and now they're in the ashes. The same verse says those who once ate delicacies are destitute in the streets. It's a hard turn from rich color to gray ash.

The answer is True. The poet says the punishment of the daughter of his people "…is greater than that of Sodom…" Sodom was overthrown in an instant (Lamentations 4:6), and the LORD rained sulfur and fire on it (Genesis 19:24). That's a hard thing to say, friends. I think he's showing how heavy his people's punishment is.

The answer is blacker than soot. The poet says, "But now their appearance is blacker than soot; they are not recognized in the streets." (Lamentations 4:8). Before, they were brighter than snow and whiter than milk. Now they're darker than soot. The swing from bright to black is the whole sadness of it.

The answer is False. The poet says, "they are not recognized in the streets." (Lamentations 4:8). Their appearance is blacker than soot. Their skin has shriveled on their bones and become "…as dry as a stick."

The answer is those slain by the sword. The poet says, "Those slain by the sword are better off than those who die of hunger, who waste away, pierced with pain because the fields lack produce." (Lamentations 4:9). It's a hard line, friends. He says the fields lack produce. That's the pain he's naming.

The answer is foundations. The poet says the LORD "…has kindled a fire in Zion, and it has consumed her foundations." (Lamentations 4:11). A foundation is what everything else sits on, so this fire reached deep. This is the end of the first half of the poem.

The answer is her prophets and her priests. The poet says, "…this was for the sins of her prophets and the guilt of her priests, who shed the blood of the righteous in her midst." (Lamentations 4:13). Prophets and priests are the ones he names. He says it plainly and doesn't soften it.

The answer is Unclean. The men shout, "Go away! Unclean!" and then, "Away, away! Do not touch us!" (Lamentations 4:15). The ones they shout at are wandering blind, defiled by blood. So people won't even touch their garments. It's a lonely picture, friends.

The answer is False. They're not welcomed. The poet says, "So they fled and wandered. Among the nations it was said, “They can stay here no longer.”" (Lamentations 4:15). They fled and wandered. That's a hard road.

The answer is that they are shown no honor. The poet says, "The priests are shown no honor; the elders find no favor." (Lamentations 4:16). The verse begins with the presence of the LORD scattering them. So the honor being gone is part of the same sad picture.

The answer is False. That nation could not save them. The poet says, "All the while our eyes were failing as we looked in vain for help. We watched from our towers for a nation that could not save us." (Lamentations 4:17). They watched for help that couldn't save them. I think that's a heavy thing to read.

The answer is the eagles in the sky. The poet says, "Those who chased us were swifter than the eagles in the sky…" (Lamentations 4:19). An eagle moves fast, and these pursuers were swifter. They pursued the people over the mountains and ambushed them in the wilderness.

The answer is that they would live under his shadow. The poet says, "We had said of him, “Under his shadow we will live among the nations.”" (Lamentations 4:20). They counted on the LORD's anointed to cover them. Then he was captured in their pits. That's a hard fall for a hope, friends.

The answer is that she will get drunk and expose herself. The poet says, "Yet the cup will pass to you as well; you will get drunk and expose yourself." (Lamentations 4:21). The Daughter of Edom is told to rejoice and be glad. Yet the cup will pass to her too.

The answer is True. The poet says, "O Daughter of Zion, your punishment is complete; He will not prolong your exile." (Lamentations 4:22). After all the dark verses, here's a word of hope, friends. The punishment is complete. The exile won't be stretched out.

The answer is False. The poet says, "But He will punish your iniquity, O Daughter of Edom; He will expose your sins." (Lamentations 4:22). So Edom's rejoicing won't be the end of her story. It's a sobering way to end the poem.
